chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
title: Playing in a small band versus a big band, with Ed Hall for five years
summary: Crawford says a small-band drummer is exposed and must fit in with taste and touch, and he took only breaks in Ed Hall's band for about five years.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: But did you -- what is the difference that you see between playing for a small band and playing for a big band?

Altogether a great difference. A great difference. You're exposed on every number, everything you play. Drums are only about six or seven pieces. Big band, you got a whole lot of help. But there's a big difference.
So do you think that the small -- a guy playing in a small band has to have his technical things in better shape? Is that what you're saying?
Yeah, he was exposed more.
Because he's not --

It's rough, but this small band drummer really got to hold up his drums. In other words, play your drums to fit in accordingly with the other musicians -- trombone, trumpet, piano and bass, clarinet, maybe five to seven pieces, mostly five -- piano, drummer, bass player, trumpet, trombone and clarinet, from five to seven pieces.
Did you use the set differently? Did you play the cymbals more or less, or you used to play more the snare drum, more or less?
No, you've got to fit yourself in and play your cymbals, but play them accordingly, taste and touch. I was no technical drummer then.
Oh, I see what you're saying, because when you don't have that volume of the big band, then that's --
Help, I call it. Yes, and so, it's a difference.
To keep from overbearing the --
Yes. Well, do you think we --

Let's see, we've got the end of this one and we've got about a half hour more. I can talk with you about your experiences in your shows and stuff, and we'll just about have finished it up. I think we will have finished it. We're almost at the end of this one.
So you were saying that you've got to have more control -- you're saying in a certain sense, you have to have more control in a smaller --
Yeah.
You have to have more dynamic.
Yes. No, not dynamic-wise, just fit in. It's a close knitted thing there, because every instrument stands out within itself, every instrument.
Did you take [many] solos when you were working in Hall's band?
In Ed Hall's -- no, I didn't know how
to. I'd take breaks, but seles --
(End of Side Two.)
-- Jimmy Crawford, last section. All right, now, when you got out of the service, you worked with Ed Hall's band.
Uh-huh.
And how long did you work in that band?
Oh, about five years, both uptown in cafe society and downtown in Cafe Society.
Had -- around that time, when you got out of the service, -- what year did you get out of the service, do you remember?
